info.name: Blog API
info.description:
# Blog API

End-to-end test suite for the **blogApi** service behind `fullStackBlog`.

## How it works

Authentication is **cookie based**: `POST /api/auth/login` sets the `access_token` and `refresh_token` httpOnly cookies, and Postman's cookie jar replays them on every later request. There is deliberately **no Bearer token** anywhere in this collection, because the API never accepts one.

The requests are ordered as a single happy path with failure cases woven in, so **Run Collection** top to bottom and every assertion passes on a fresh database.

| Folder | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| `00 · Health Check` | Service is up |
| `01 · Authentication` | Register, log in, rotate the access token |
| `02 · User Profile` | Read the profile, change username/email, change password, prove the new password works |
| `03 · Blog Posts` | Create, list, list own, read, update |
| `04 · Comments` | Create, list, delete |
| `05 · Validation & Error Handling` | Every `400` / `404` / `401` path |
| `06 · Session Recovery` | Re-establish a valid session after the negative tests |
| `07 · Ownership Checks` | A second user cannot touch somebody else's post (`403`) |
| `08 · Teardown` | Back to the author, delete the post, confirm it is gone |
| `09 · Logout` | Clear the cookies and prove the session is closed |

## Why a second user exists

`07 · Ownership Checks` signs in as a different account, so the `403` responses are produced by real authorisation logic rather than by mocked data. The suite signs back in as the original author afterwards.

## Why `Logout` is the last folder

Logging out clears both auth cookies, so every request after it would run unauthenticated. It is placed last, followed by one request that asserts the session really is closed.

## Running it

```bash
# The API must already be running.
npm test                                        # against http://localhost:3000
npm test -- --env-var baseUrl=http://host:port  # against another host
```

In the Postman app: **Import** this file, then **Run Collection**.

Every run generates a fresh set of credentials, so the collection is safe to re-run against a database that already holds data from a previous run.

item.name: 00 · Health Check
item.description: Render polls this path to decide the service is up, so it is also the quickest way to confirm the API is reachable.

request.description: Public liveness probe. Expects `200` and a plain-text greeting.

exec: pm.test("The response is fast enough to be a real health check", () => {

item.name: 01 · Authentication
item.description: Account creation and the cookie-based session. No token is returned in the body — the cookies are the whole mechanism.

request.description:
Creates an account and returns the password-free user with `201`.

Credentials are generated here, in the first request that needs them, so a re-run never collides with the accounts a previous run created.

exec: // A fresh identity per run. Base36 of the current timestamp is short,
// lowercase and alphanumeric, which satisfies the username pattern.
pm.test("Response contains the new user id", () => {
pm.test("Response echoes the submitted username and email", () => {
pm.test("Registering does not open a session", () => {

request.description: Exchanges credentials for the token pair. The body carries only the user; the tokens arrive as httpOnly cookies that Postman stores and replays automatically.

exec: pm.test("Access token is issued as an httpOnly cookie", () => {
pm.test("Refresh token is issued as an httpOnly cookie", () => {
pm.test("No token leaks into the response body", () => {

request.description: Rotates the access token using the still-valid refresh cookie. This is what lets the client stay signed in after the 15-minute access token expires.

exec: pm.test("Response confirms a new access token", () => {
pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("A new access token has been issued");
pm.test("A replacement access token cookie is set", () => {
pm.test("The refresh cookie is not rotated, only the access token", () => {

item.name: 02 · User Profile
item.description: Profile reads and writes for the authenticated user, including a password change that is re-hashed server-side.

exec: pm.test("The rotated access token is accepted", () => {

request.description: A real request fired straight after the access cookie was replaced, proving the rotated token is the one the API accepts. This replaces an in-script sub-request, which cannot be trusted to be anonymous.
Returns the caller's own profile, resolved from the access token rather than from anything the client sends.

exec: pm.test("Profile belongs to the authenticated user", () => {

request.description: Partial update. Only the fields that are sent are validated and written, so `password` can be left out entirely.

exec: // Later requests sign in with the new credentials.

request.description: Sends a **plain** password. The API must hash it before writing, which the next request proves by logging in with it.

exec: pm.test("Response does not leak the new password", () => {

request.description: Regression check for the password round-trip: if the value had been stored in plain text, or hashed twice, this login would fail with `401`.

exec: pm.test("Sign in works with the updated credentials", () => {

item.description: Comment thread for the post created above. Reads are public; writes require a token and are restricted to the comment's author.

request.description: Adds a comment to the post. The API resolves the post first, so a comment can never be attached to a post that does not exist.

exec: pm.test("Response contains the new comment id", () => {
pm.test("Content and parent post are stored as submitted", () => {
pm.test("The commenter is the authenticated user", () => {

pm.test("The thread is sorted newest first", () => {

exec: pm.test("The deleted comment is echoed back", () => {

item.name: 05 · Validation & Error Handling
item.description: Every rejection path the API is supposed to produce. These run while the session is still valid, so they exercise validation and authorisation rather than missing credentials.

request.description: The password fails the strength policy: shorter than 8 characters and missing an uppercase letter, a number and a symbol.

exec: pm.test("The password field is named in the error", () => {
pm.test("The response follows the standard error shape", () => {

request.description: Everything else is valid, so the `400` can only come from the email format check.

exec: pm.test("The email field is named in the error", () => {

request.description: The validation pipe runs with `whitelist` and `forbidNonWhitelisted`, so a field the DTO does not declare is refused instead of being silently dropped or persisted. This is what stops mass-assignment.

exec: pm.test("The unknown field is named in the error", () => {

request.description: Registers the account from `01 · Authentication` a second time. Mongo's duplicate-key error is translated into a `400` so it never surfaces as a `500`.

exec: pm.test("A duplicate is reported as a bad request, not a crash", () => {
pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("An account with this username or email already exists");

request.description: Without the id pipe, Mongoose would raise a `CastError` and Nest would turn it into a meaningless `500`. The pipe turns it into a `400` instead.

exec: pm.test("The malformed id is rejected with a readable message", () => {

request.description: An empty comment is refused by the DTO before it reaches the database.

exec: pm.test("The content field is named in the error", () => {

request.description: A syntactically valid ObjectId that matches nothing. The API must answer `404`, not `400` and not an empty `200`.

exec: pm.test("A missing post is reported clearly", () => {

exec: pm.test("The already deleted comment is reported as missing", () => {

Correct username, wrong password. The generic message is the same one an unknown account receives, so login cannot be used to enumerate users.

pm.test("No session cookie is issued on a failed login", () => {

exec: pm.test("An unknown account is indistinguishable from a wrong password", () => {

item.name: 06 · Session Recovery
item.description: Re-establishes a clean session after the negative tests, and re-asserts that the cookies still work.

request.description: Logs the post author back in with the credentials set in `02 · User Profile`.

exec: pm.test("The post author is signed in again", () => {

item.name: 07 · Ownership Checks
item.description: A second account is created and signed in so the authorisation rules are exercised against a real, different user rather than a simulated one.

request.description: Generates the second identity used by the `403` assertions.

exec: pm.test("The second user is a distinct account", () => {

request.description: Replaces the session cookies, so everything after this request runs as the second user. `08 · Teardown` signs the author back in.

exec: pm.test("The session now belongs to the second user", () => {

request.description: Authenticated, but not the author. The API answers `403` — not `404` — so the caller can tell "not yours" apart from "not there".

exec: pm.test("The refusal names the action that was refused", () => {
pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("You are not allowed to update this post");

request.description: The same rule on the destructive path. `08 · Teardown` proves the post is still there afterwards.

exec: pm.test("The refusal names the action that was refused", () => {
pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("You are not allowed to delete this post");
pm.test("The post is still owned by its author", () => {

request.description: Reads the post back as a real request to prove the refused delete had no side effect.

item.name: 200 · Own Feed Is Empty For The Second User

request.description: Proof that ownership filtering is real: the second user has no posts, because the post belongs to somebody else.

exec: pm.test("The other author's post is not in this feed", () => {

item.name: 08 · Teardown
item.description: Signs the author back in and removes the post created at the start of the run, leaving the database as it was found.

request.description: Only the author may delete the post, so the author has to be the one signed in.
Author-only delete, returning `200` and the removed post.

exec: pm.test("The removed post is echoed back", () => {

request.description: Confirms the delete actually removed the document, rather than only reporting success.

exec: pm.test("The deleted post is reported as missing", () => {

item.name: 09 · Logout
item.description: Signs the author out for real. Everything after this point runs with no session at all, which is the only trustworthy way to prove the guards actually reject anonymous callers.

request.description: Clears both auth cookies using the exact attributes they were set with, which is what makes the browser actually drop them.

The final assertion of the run: after logout the same request that succeeded in `02 · User Profile` is refused. Fired out of band so the assertion is about the API, not about the cookie jar's bookkeeping.

item.name: 10 · Session Is Closed
item.description: Runs after Logout, so there is no cookie to send. A 200 here would mean a protected route accepted an anonymous caller. These replace sub-requests, which inherit the signed-in cookie jar and therefore cannot test anonymity at all.

exec: pm.test("The guard names the missing session", () => {

request.description: No cookie is sent because the session was closed in the previous folder.
Logout cleared the refresh cookie, so the refresh strategy must reject the request.
